meta.name: Grand Theft After-Dark — the run-up calendar
meta.what: 122 daily posts narrated by TJ, from launch to the first event. Day 122 is event day, so the calendar is countdown-relative — shift it to whatever November date the show lands on.
meta.cadence: 7 a week until the first event. After that the tour starts and live footage takes over: drop to 3 a week (see tourCadence).
phases: Days 1–7 · the offer — what this is, the vault, the four keys, why you
Days 8–31 · the city — the four districts, the dial, the texture of the world
Days 32–61 · the families — the fifty years that made this inevitable
Days 62–92 · the heat — the keys move, the gala is announced, tickets go up
Days 93–99 · final approach — three weeks out, everybody's committed
Days 100–122 · the countdown — the crews, the people, the games, the ask
meta.shootNote: 122 posts is not 122 shoots. Seven recurring formats means you batch: one lighting setup, one wardrobe, twenty RAP SHEETs in an afternoon. Shoot a month ahead, always.

formats.name: TRANSMISSION
formats.what: TJ straight to camera about the night itself. The offer, the ask, the stakes. The only format that sells.

formats.name: CITY RECORDS
formats.what: A piece of the fifty-year history. TJ over archive-feel b-roll — no face needed, batch the VO.

formats.name: RAP SHEET
formats.what: One character, one file. Name, crew, known for, one story. The most batchable format you have.

formats.name: OVERHEARD
formats.what: One line somebody said, then TJ explains what it meant. Shortest format, highest share rate.

formats.name: THE DIAL
formats.what: The music. What each crew sounds like and why. Your natural territory — shoot these behind the decks.

formats.name: EVIDENCE
formats.what: McGraw's case. A photo, a file, a dead end. This is the format that carries the myth.

formats.name: HOUSE RULES
formats.what: Practical. What the night is, what to wear, how it works. Kills objections and drives tickets.

shape: 0:00–0:03  HOOK — TJ already mid-thought. One line that opens a question.
0:03–0:20  THE LORE — exactly one fact about the world. Never two.
0:20–0:45  THE TURN — tie it to the room, the night, or the viewer.
0:45–0:60  THE ASK — one action. Never two.
hookRules: Start mid-sentence. Never 'hey guys', never 'welcome to', never say the format's name.
Lead with a number, a name, or a contradiction.
Say the thing that sounds like it shouldn't be said out loud.
The on-screen text is NOT the spoken line — it's the punch under it.
If the first frame needs context to make sense, it's not a hook.
craft: Shot to camera, TJ lit hard against black with one neon rim in the crew's colour.
Hard cut in — no logo sting at the front. Brand at the END or nowhere.
Burned-in captions always: most of this is watched on mute.
9:16, one idea per post. If it needs two, it's two posts.
Period film look for the world b-roll (1977–1983); TJ himself is present-day.

shareEngine.principle: Nobody shares an advert for a party. They share a thing that says something about them, a thing that settles an argument, or a thing they can't believe.

mechanisms.name: Identity — pick a colour
mechanisms.why: Choosing a faction is a self-description, and self-descriptions get posted. Four crews means four tribes recruiting for you, for free.

mechanisms.name: Argument — my crew beats your crew
mechanisms.why: Rivalry is the cheapest engagement there is. Every crew post is written to bait the other three.

mechanisms.name: Secret — never explain the myth
mechanisms.why: Sharing a mystery signals you're on the inside. The moment it's explained, it stops moving.

mechanisms.name: Tag-a-friend — the characters are people they know
mechanisms.why: Vinnie, Problem and Kayleigh exist to be someone's mate, someone's cousin, someone's colleague. This is the format that escapes your own audience.

mechanisms.name: Disbelief — the tiger
mechanisms.why: An animal outsmarting two crime families is the single most forwardable thing in this world. Do not overthink it, do not over-explain it.

mechanisms.name: Flex — you're made now
mechanisms.why: The crew card, the member number and the leaderboard are post-event proof. The audience makes the recap content for you.

shareEngine.cadence: One post a day for 30 days, timed to land on the event. Day 15 and day 28 are the two to put money behind — 15 because the crews are all established by then, 28 because it's the payoff.
shareEngine.reply: TJ replies in character, always. Never break it. A comment answered by the Handler is worth more than a hundred impressions, and people screenshot it.
shareEngine.ugc: After the night: repost the room's own footage under the same voice. The crowd becomes the cast, which is the whole thesis of the show anyway.

tourCadence.when: From the first event onward. Live footage exists now, so the job changes from building a world to proving it happened.
tourCadence.volume: 3 posts a week, down from 7. The drop is not a retreat — one post with real crowd footage outperforms four scripted ones, and the tour eats the time you were spending writing.

theThree.what: Last show's best 30 seconds. Real crowd, real noise, the moment the room lost it. No narration needed — let it be loud.
theThree.why: This is the ad. Nothing you can write beats a wide shot of 800 phones going up at once.

theThree.what: TJ to camera, same as always — a piece of lore, a character, or the next city's story. Keeps the serial alive between shows.
theThree.why: The voice is the brand. Losing it between tour dates costs you the thing you spent four months building.

theThree.what: Next city, next date, tickets. Built on a clip from the last one so the ask is evidence-led, not a poster.
theThree.why: Announcing a date over footage of the last show converts several times better than announcing a date.

tourCadence.reuse: Everything in this calendar that isn't tied to the first event is evergreen — the history, the characters, the dial. A new city gets the run-up again, compressed to 6 weeks, with the proof clips from the shows you've already done cut in.
tourCadence.ugc: Once there's an audience in the room, they make the PROOF slot for you. Repost with the Handler's voice over the top and it stays on-brand while costing you nothing.

posts.title: What After-Dark Is
posts.hook: There's a vault in this city with eight figures in it, and in fifty years nobody's opened it.
posts.script:
There's a vault in this city with eight figures in it, and in fifty years nobody has opened it.
Not because they can't find it. Everybody knows where it is.
Because of how it locks — and I'll get to that.
My name's TJ. Four gangs run this city and all four of them want what's in that room. On the night, they're all going to be in the same building trying to take it.
So are you.
That's Grand Theft After-Dark. Follow this, because from here I'm telling you the whole thing — who they are, how it works, and how you end up in the middle of it.
shots: gloved hand on wet glass, neon
aerial over four glowing districts
a vault door, one hard light
posts.caption: Fifty years. Nobody's opened it. That changes on one night. #GrandTheftAfterDark
posts.cta: Follow — the whole story drops daily.
posts.shareTrigger: Curiosity gap: a locked thing with a reason nobody's guessed yet.

posts.title: The Vault
posts.hook: Everybody asks me what's actually in the vault. Wrong question.
posts.script:
Everybody asks me what's actually in the vault. That's the wrong question.
The right question is why nobody's ever got it out.
It's eight figures. It's been eight figures the whole time. It sits under a building downtown that nobody photographs, and the men who put it there are fifty years dead.
They didn't trust each other. Not one of them, not for a second. So they didn't build a safe — they built an argument, and they made it out of steel.
Tomorrow I'll show you what that means.
shots: macro: steel vault door seams
dust in a hard overhead beam
an empty concrete chamber, distant
posts.caption: It's not a safe. It's an argument made out of steel.
posts.shareTrigger: Cliffhanger — a promise with a date on it.

posts.title: Four Keys
posts.hook: The vault takes four keys. That's the whole problem.
posts.script:
The vault takes four keys.
Four colours, four turns, and every one of them has to happen inside the same minute. Miss the window and the whole thing re-locks for another day.
One key each went to the four families that built this city. Gold. Pink. Cyan. Violet.
Which means no crew in this city can open that vault alone. Not the oldest one, not the richest one, not the one with the tiger.
They need each other.
They have never hated anything more in their lives.
shots: four coloured key-turns, macro, no faces
four lit windows in four districts
a four-colour lock ring glowing
posts.caption: Four keys. Four crews. Nobody gets it alone. Which one are you? #GTAD
posts.cta: Gold, pink, cyan or violet — comment your colour.
posts.shareTrigger: Identity + argument: people pick a side and defend it.

posts.title: Why Tonight
posts.hook: The President is throwing a party in the same building as the vault. Nobody thinks that's an accident.
posts.script:
The President is throwing a gala. He's calling it a night of unity — a city standing together against crime. There'll be a podium, a banner, and a man in a navy suit telling a room full of criminals how tough he is on criminals.
The gala is in the building. The vault is in that building.
Every crew got an invitation. And every crew knows the other three got one too.
One night. One room. All four keys in the same place for the first time in fifty years.
Nobody thinks that's an accident. Nobody can prove it isn't.
shots: WAR ON CRIME banner over a podium
four-colour ballroom, distant blurred crowd
a motorcade gliding past, distant
posts.caption: A night of unity, he's calling it. In the same building as the vault. Sure.
posts.shareTrigger: Conspiracy hook — invites the audience to spot the setup.

posts.title: Why You
posts.hook: Four crews are recruiting off the floor that night. That's not a metaphor.
posts.script:
Here's the part the four of them don't advertise.
A key gets you a turn. It doesn't get you the room.
Four crews, one night, and not one of them has enough hands — not enough people to hold a floor, run a job, move a package, or crack a four-colour code while three other crews are doing the same thing.
So all four of them are recruiting. In that building. Off that floor. From whoever shows up.
That's you. You pick a colour at the door and you're theirs for the night.
You're not watching this one. You're in it.
shots: a crowded neon floor, faces out of focus
a hand taking a coloured wristband
four colour-lit crowd pockets
posts.caption: You don't watch this one. You get recruited.
posts.cta: Pick your colour at the door.
posts.shareTrigger: Participation promise — the reason to bring people.

posts.title: The Two Rules
posts.hook: There are two rules that night and I'm only saying them once.
posts.script:
There are two rules that night. I'm only saying them once.
Don't get wasted.
Don't get busted.
That's it. That's the list.
And I know how simple that sounds. Every single night, somebody in that building manages to break both of them before midnight, and every single night it's the one who told me they wouldn't.
Everything else — the crews, the keys, the vault, the games — all of that is going to be explained to you by people who are lying to you.
The only voice in that room you can trust is coming out of the booth.
That's me.
shots: TJ to camera, hard key, black three-piece
booth silhouette, magenta rim light
crowd, hands up, motion blur
posts.caption: Don't get wasted. Don't get busted. That's the whole list.
posts.shareTrigger: A chantable catchphrase — the room repeats it, the comments repeat it.

posts.title: The Man With No Face
posts.hook: Ask any of the four who really runs this city and watch what happens to their face.
posts.script:
Ask any of the four crews who really runs this city. Watch what happens.
They go quiet.
Then, if they like you, they'll tell you about a man in a black three-piece suit who has never been photographed. Black gloves. Always turned away.
The Corvettis are certain he takes a cut. Rico swears he's been inside the house. The Firm has a file on him with nothing in it.
Four crews. Four keys. And every one of them looking over their shoulder at a man none of them can name.
I'd tell you what I know.
You should probably hear that part in person.
shots: black-gloved hand, extreme close, wet neon
CCTV static over a dark lobby
a lit penthouse window from far below
posts.caption: Four crews. Not one of them will say his name out loud.
posts.cta: Who do you think he is?
posts.shareTrigger: Secret-keeping — sharing signals you're in on something.

posts.title: Four Towns
posts.hook: This was never one city. It was four towns that grew until they touched.
posts.script:
This was never one city.
It was four towns — the docks, the marina, the block and the flats — and they grew until they touched, and then they kept growing.
By the time anybody drew a single line around all four and gave it one name, the families were already in place.
So when people ask me who runs this city, that's the wrong question too.
Nobody runs it. Four people run a quarter each, and they've spent fifty years pretending that's the same thing.
shots: aerial over four glowing districts, night
an old map, four hand-drawn borders
posts.caption: It was four towns before it was one city. That never really stopped.
posts.shareTrigger: Local-identity hook — people map it onto their own city.

posts.title: The Gold Docks
posts.hook: The oldest money in this city still smells like fish and diesel.
posts.script:
The docks came first.
Old stone, wet cobbles, bistro lights strung between buildings that were warehouses before they were restaurants.
The oldest money in this city still smells faintly of fish and diesel, and the people who have it would rather you didn't mention that.
This is Corvetti ground. Has been for three generations.
You'll know when you're on it, because everybody gets quieter.
shots: gold-lit waterfront, wet cobbles, harbour fog
hanging bistro lights, slow push
posts.caption: The oldest money here still smells like the docks.
posts.shareTrigger: District identity: gives the gold faction a home to claim.

posts.title: We Just Rent It
posts.hook: "It's nobody's city, boy. We just rent it." That's the most honest thing anyone's said all year.
posts.script:
Overheard on the pier, from a man in his seventies, to a man half his age who'd just claimed the whole city was his.
"It's nobody's city, boy. We just rent it."
And then he looked up. At one lit window, high above the water.
And he said: from him.
That's the most honest thing anybody in this city has said all year, and the man who said it is the last person you'd expect to admit it.
shots: rain pier at night, two figures squaring off
one lit penthouse window, very high up
posts.caption: "It's nobody's city, boy. We just rent it. …From him."
posts.shareTrigger: Mystery + a quotable line — the two things that travel.

posts.title: Four Stations
posts.hook: This city has four radio stations and every one of them belongs to somebody dangerous.
posts.script:
Four crews. Four stations.
Gold Standard Radio, AM 10.40 — nothing but the classics, nothing but respect.
La Onda, 98.6 — the loudest signal on the water.
Radio Los Santos, 106 — the block, the beat and the bounce.
And 88.8 The Firm, which does not take requests, because it plays what's optimal.
On the night, whichever crew is up, that's what the room sounds like.
You'll feel the station change before anybody tells you it has.
shots: a radio dial sweeping four colours
four crowd pockets under four colour washes
posts.caption: Four crews. Four stations. You'll hear the city change hands.
posts.cta: Which station are you tuned to?
posts.shareTrigger: Music identity — the audience's real entry point.

posts.title: What You're Actually Buying
posts.hook: People keep asking if it's a club night or a show. It's neither, and that's the point.
posts.onScreenText: IT'S A HEIST. YOU'RE IN IT.
posts.script:
People keep asking whether this is a club night or a show.
It's neither, and that's the whole point.
There's a film. There are four crews. There's a vault. And there are twelve games that the entire building plays at the same time, on their phones, on the floor.
You don't sit and watch it, and you don't just dance through it. You get recruited, you pick a colour, and by the end of the night you either opened that vault or you watched somebody else do it.
That's what you're buying.
shots: wide floor, hundreds of phones lit
screens above a packed crowd
posts.caption: Not a club night. Not a show. You get recruited.
posts.cta: Save this for whoever keeps asking.
posts.shareTrigger: Answers the actual objection — saveable, so it gets sent.

posts.title: The Board
posts.hook: There's a detective in this city with a wall of photographs and one empty space in the middle.
posts.script:
There's a detective in this city who's been on the same case for twenty years.
He's got a wall. Photographs, string, four columns — one for each crew — and every face on it he can name.
Except one space. Middle of the board. Empty.
Twenty years and he has never once been able to put a photograph in it.
He knows the man exists because of the shape of the hole he leaves.
That's the whole case. That's what Dutch McGraw has.
shots: a corkboard, four columns, one gap
string and pins, macro, low light
posts.caption: Twenty years. One empty space in the middle of the board.
posts.shareTrigger: Invites theorising — the comments write themselves.

posts.title: What The Night Looks Like
posts.hook: You walk in, somebody hands you a colour, and you're in a gang. That's minute one.
posts.onScreenText: MINUTE ONE: YOU'RE IN A GANG.
posts.script:
Here's what actually happens.
You walk in. Before you get to the bar, somebody hands you a colour — gold, pink, cyan or violet — and that's your crew for the night.
The story plays on the screens between the music. Every so often it stops and somebody hands you a job, and every phone in the room lights up at once.
You play. Your colour scores. The board goes up.
No stage. No queue. No getting picked on.
Just you, your phone, and three other crews you now have a problem with.
shots: a wristband going on at the door
a leaderboard flipping over, four colours
posts.caption: Minute one, you're in a gang. That's how it starts.
posts.shareTrigger: Removes fear, adds a plus-one prompt.

posts.title: Off The Boats
posts.hook: The first Corvetti in this city arrived with a suitcase and a grudge.
posts.script:
The first Corvetti arrived here with a suitcase and a grudge.
He took work on the docks because that's what there was, and inside four years he owned the part of the docks nobody was watching.
He never raised his voice, he never wrote anything down, and he never once asked for anything twice.
His grandson runs the family now the exact same way.
That's not tradition. In this city, that's a business model that has outlived three police commissioners.
shots: an old suitcase on wet stone
a warehouse door, gold light spilling
posts.caption: A suitcase and a grudge. Three generations later they still don't write anything down.
posts.shareTrigger: Origin myth — factions love a founding story.

posts.title: The Pink Marina
posts.hook: There's a district in this city you can see from three miles away. That's deliberate.
posts.script:
You can see the marina from three miles away. That is entirely deliberate.
Black yachts, palm trees, and a mirrored mansion up on the rise with the lights left on whether anybody's home or not.
This is Halcón ground. Nothing here is hidden, nothing here is understated, and nothing here is an accident.
The Corvettis think it's vulgar.
The Halcóns think being seen is the whole point of having anything.
shots: hot-pink neon marina, black yachts
a mirrored mansion glowing through rain
posts.caption: You can see it from three miles out. On purpose.
posts.shareTrigger: Direct rivalry bait at the gold faction.

posts.title: What's The Drop
posts.hook: A grown man asked his father what the drop was. In front of people.
posts.script:
A grown man asked his father, out loud, in front of other people, what the drop was.
And his father — who has buried better men for less — put down a cannoli, looked at him for a long time, and said: respect.
And also the drop.
I want to be clear that this family is the most feared organisation in this city.
And that man is next in line.
shots: a cannoli on a checkered cloth, macro
a sweating man in an open collar
posts.caption: "Pop… what's the drop?" A question you ask exactly once.
posts.shareTrigger: Family-tag comedy, the highest-travel format.

posts.title: Gold Standard
posts.hook: This crew's entire sound is men in suits singing about women who left them.
posts.script:
Gold Standard Radio. AM 10.40.
This is the Corvetti sound, and it hasn't changed since 1962. Rat-Pack swing. Crooners. Doo-wop. Big brass when things are going well and a single sad string section when they're not.
It's men in beautiful suits singing about women who left them, and underneath all of it there's something with teeth.
That's the trick of that whole family in one sound.
It's warm right up until it isn't.
shots: vinyl crackle, a turntable, warm gold light
an empty velvet back room, slow push
posts.caption: Warm right up until it isn't. That's the whole family in one sound.
posts.shareTrigger: Music request = comments, and you're a DJ. Free content.

posts.title: Not Extras
posts.hook: You're not the audience at this thing. You're the labour.
posts.script:
Let me be blunt about your role in this.
You're not the audience. Four crews are walking into that building and not one of them has enough people to do what they're planning.
They need hands. To hold a floor, run a job, move a package, crack a code against three other crews doing exactly the same thing.
So they recruit. Off the floor. From whoever turned up.
You're not extras in somebody else's night.
You're the reason it can happen at all.
shots: a crowded floor from above, four colour pockets
a hand taking a coloured band
posts.caption: You're not the audience. You're the labour. #GTAD
posts.shareTrigger: Flattery + purpose — makes people want a role.

posts.title: The Empty File
posts.hook: The richest crew in this city built a file on him. I've read it. It's empty.
posts.script:
The Firm builds a file on everybody. It's most of what they actually do.
They've got one on him.
No name. No photograph. No date of birth, no known associates, no last known address.
What's in it is a list of things that happened that nobody can explain, going back further than anybody working there has been alive.
The most data-obsessed crew in this city has one folder with nothing in it.
And they will not throw it away.
shots: a manila folder opening on nothing
violet monitor glow on an empty desk
posts.caption: The most data-obsessed crew in the city has one empty file. And they keep it.
posts.shareTrigger: Mystery — never explained, so it keeps circulating.

posts.title: What To Wear
posts.hook: Dress like you're in one of the four crews. Nobody's checking, everybody's looking.
posts.script:
What to wear.
Gold if you want the old money look — a good jacket, something that gleams.
Pink if you plan to be seen from across the room, which is the entire Halcón philosophy.
Cyan if you're here to be comfortable and still outlast everybody.
Violet if you own one very expensive black turtleneck and you've been waiting for a reason.
Nobody's on the door checking.
But I promise you, everybody in that room is looking.
shots: four outfits under four colour washes
a crowd, colour-blocked, wide
posts.caption: Gold, pink, cyan or violet. Nobody's checking. Everybody's looking.
posts.shareTrigger: Outfit posts drive tagging and group planning.

posts.title: The Block
posts.hook: One crew in this city never wanted more than the twelve streets they grew up on.
posts.script:
Every crew in this story wanted the whole city.
Except one.
The Street Kings have never made a move outside twelve streets, and those twelve streets are the only part of this city where people are genuinely, uncomplicatedly glad to see the crew that runs them.
The other three have never understood it. They keep waiting for the expansion.
It isn't coming.
Marcus Wells worked out something the rest of them haven't: it's easier to hold something people want you to have.
shots: cyan-lit corner store, murals, wet asphalt
a lowrider parked, hydraulics settling
posts.caption: Twelve streets. They never wanted more. That's why they still have them.
posts.shareTrigger: Underdog appeal; the easiest faction to root for.

posts.title: The Cyan Block
posts.hook: Nobody in this district got frightened into anything. That makes it the hardest one to take.
posts.script:
The block.
Murals, corner stores, hydraulics, and the best three minutes of music in any room the Street Kings walk into.
Here's what makes it the hardest district in the city to move on: nobody here got frightened into anything.
You can lean on people who were coerced. You can buy people who were bought.
You can't do much with a neighbourhood that actually likes who runs it.
The other three crews have tried. It's the one thing all three of them have failed at.
shots: cyan-lit block at night, steam from a grate
a convoy of chrome pulling out
posts.caption: You can't lean on a neighbourhood that likes who runs it.
posts.shareTrigger: Values-based identity — the crew you join to be a good guy.

posts.title: A Legendary Honda
posts.hook: Somebody suggested boosting the getaway car might be his origin story. It's a Honda.
posts.script:
Overheard on the block.
One member of a serious criminal organisation floating the idea that he personally should boost the getaway car — that it might, and I'm quoting, be his origin story.
His boss, without any real cruelty, pointed out that it's a Honda.
And he said — and this is the part I keep thinking about —
A legendary Honda.
That man is going to be at this event. He's going to be at all of them.
shots: a beat-up Honda under neon, hero angle
a man mid-laugh, cyan light, holding food
posts.caption: "…A *legendary* Honda."
posts.cta: Tag whoever this is in your group.
posts.shareTrigger: Pure comedy — the clip that escapes your following.

posts.title: Radio Los Santos
posts.hook: This is the only station in the city that nobody argues about.
posts.script:
Radio Los Santos, 106.
The block, the beat and the bounce. G-funk, lowrider oldies, Chicano soul, talkbox, and the coolest groove in any building it gets played in.
Here's the thing about the cyan station.
Every other crew in this city will tell you their sound is the best one. And every one of them, privately, likes this station.
It's the only signal in this city nobody argues about.
When it drops, the whole room agrees for about four minutes.
shots: a lowrider on hydraulics, cyan glow
a packed floor moving as one, wide
posts.caption: The only station in this city nobody argues about.
posts.cta: Name one that belongs on it.
posts.shareTrigger: Music tribalism + request bait.

posts.title: Pick Early
posts.hook: You'll pick a colour at the door. I'd think about it before then.
posts.script:
You get one choice at that door and you're stuck with it all night.
Gold, if you think power should be quiet.
Pink, if you have never once been the quietest person in a room.
Cyan, if your friends actually like you.
Violet, if you've read the terms and conditions and found a way through them.
And before you tell me you'll decide when you get there — you won't. You'll pick whatever your mate picks, and then you'll spend the whole night defending it.
So think about it now.
shots: four wristbands on four wrists
a door with four coloured lights above it
posts.caption: Gold, pink, cyan or violet. At the door it's final. #GTAD
posts.shareTrigger: THE identity post — repeatable monthly, always performs.

posts.title: The Photograph
posts.hook: There is one photograph of him in existence and you can't see him in it.
posts.script:
There's one photograph.
Taken outside a restaurant on the docks, nineteen years ago, by somebody who didn't know what they were taking a picture of.
Four men at a table. Everybody in this city can name three of them.
And at the edge of the frame, half out of shot, there's a hand. Black glove. Resting on the back of the fourth chair.
That's it. That's the only image anybody has.
McGraw has had it enlarged eleven times.
shots: an old photo, four men at a table, edge of frame
a black-gloved hand on a chair back, macro
posts.caption: One photograph. Four men. And a hand on the fourth chair.
posts.cta: Zoom in. Tell me what you see.
posts.shareTrigger: Zoom-in bait — people literally screenshot and circle it.

posts.title: Your Phone Is The Controller
posts.hook: No app to download at the door. If you can hold a phone, you're playing.
posts.script:
The most common question I get, so let's kill it.
There is nothing to download at the door. No app store, no queue, no signing up to anything, no handing over your email to play a game.
You'll get sent to a page. It'll load. That's the whole process.
Charge your phone before you come, because you'll be on it more than you expect — and because I am not lending you mine.
If you can hold a phone and hear me, you're playing.
shots: a phone lighting up with a game card
a floor of raised phones, all glowing
posts.caption: Nothing to download. Just charge your phone.
posts.cta: Send this to the one who always asks.
posts.shareTrigger: Objection-killer, highly saveable.

posts.title: The Tower
posts.hook: In 2011 somebody bought their way into a fifty-year-old arrangement. Nobody has forgiven it.
posts.script:
Everybody else in this story inherited their place.
The Firm bought theirs.
A glass tower went up on the flats, and inside eighteen months the people in it had a seat at a table that three families had spent fifty years dying for.
They didn't fight anybody. They didn't have to. They just made it more expensive to say no than to say yes.
The other three call them tourists.
And every single one of the other three has taken their money.
shots: cold violet towers, one lit floor high up
a business card straightened, macro
posts.caption: Three families died for that seat. The Firm bought it.
posts.shareTrigger: Villain faction — being hated is engagement.

posts.title: The Violet Towers
posts.hook: The newest district in this city has no history, and they've turned that into a selling point.
posts.script:
The flats.
Cold glass, violet light, and a district with no history whatsoever — which The Firm has somehow turned into a selling point.
No old grudges. No inherited debts. No cousin you have to employ.
They'll tell you they're the only crew in this city operating without legacy drag, and the infuriating thing is that they're not entirely wrong.
They're the newest, richest, least liked crew in this story.
And they're the only one that's grown every single year.
shots: a cluster of violet glass towers, rain
a monitor wall, screen glow, no faces
posts.caption: No history. They've made that a selling point. And it's working.
posts.shareTrigger: The faction people love to argue against.

posts.title: The Rat Is You
posts.hook: Somebody asked their analyst who was leaking. She answered honestly.
posts.script:
A founder in this city ordered a full loyalty audit. Every crew, cross-referenced. He wanted to know if they could gamify it — whether the rat could be, and I'm quoting again, a subscription.
His analyst looked up exactly once and said: the rat is you. You post everything.
Then went back to her tablet.
She is paid a fraction of what he is.
She is the only reason that tower is still standing.
shots: a tablet and a raised eyebrow, no full face
violet monitor glow, an empty founder's chair
posts.caption: "The rat is you, Preston. You post everything."
posts.cta: Tag the one holding your workplace together.
posts.shareTrigger: Workplace recognition — travels far outside nightlife.

posts.title: 88.8 The Firm
posts.hook: This station doesn't take requests. It plays what's optimal.
posts.script:
88.8 The Firm.
Glossy eighties synth-pop, yacht rock, and then — without warning — cold techno with nothing human in it at all.
It is precise, expensive, and slightly soulless on purpose.
Their station ident says: we don't play requests, we play what's optimal. Crime, as a service. Terms apply.
And here's what bothers me. It's the most technically well-made sound in this city.
It's just that nobody's ever cried to it.
shots: sterile violet room, one moving light
a mixer, cold light, precise hands
posts.caption: "We don't play requests. We play what's optimal."
posts.cta: Is it a banger or is it a spreadsheet?
posts.shareTrigger: Opinion bait — an argument with a clear side.

posts.title: Fifty Years
posts.hook: Everything about this night was decided in a room in 1974 by four men who hated each other.
posts.script:
Everything about this night — the vault, the keys, the fact that all four of them have to be in the same room — was decided fifty years ago by four men who could not stand each other.
They had a problem: they'd made more money together than any one of them could safely hold.
So they built somewhere to put it.
And then they made absolutely certain that none of them could ever get it out alone.
They thought they were being careful.
What they actually did was leave this to their grandchildren.
shots: an old document, four signatures
a vault door being installed, archive feel
posts.caption: Four men who hated each other built this problem in 1974.
posts.cta: Follow — I'm telling the whole fifty years.
posts.shareTrigger: Serial promise — converts a scroller into a follower.

posts.title: The Signature
posts.hook: Three of the four signatures on that document belong to men we can name.
posts.script:
The document exists. McGraw has a copy — a bad one, third generation, but readable.
Four signatures at the bottom.
Three of them belong to men this city can name. Founders. Grandfathers. Two of them have streets named after them, which is its own kind of joke.
The fourth signature is a single letter.
Just an H.
And every expert McGraw has shown it to has told him the same thing: whoever wrote that had signed it that way their whole life.
shots: a signature line, macro, one letter
a photocopied document under a lamp
posts.caption: Three names. And one letter. H.
posts.shareTrigger: The myth advances — this is the post people bookmark.

posts.title: Is It A Rave Or A Show
posts.hook: It's a night out that happens to have a plot. You can ignore the plot. Most people don't.
posts.script:
Straight answer, because people keep asking.
It's a night out that happens to have a plot.
The music runs all night — that part is exactly what you'd expect from me. The story happens between the music, on the screens, in about a minute at a time.
You can ignore all of it and just dance. Genuinely. Nobody will bother you.
But I'll tell you what happens: about an hour in, your mate picks a colour, starts winning, and you get competitive.
Everybody says they'll ignore it. Almost nobody does.
shots: a packed dancefloor, screens above
a group leaning into one phone, laughing
posts.caption: It's a night out with a plot. You can ignore the plot. You won't.
posts.cta: Which one of you goes competitive first?
posts.shareTrigger: Group-dynamic prompt — tags friends automatically.

posts.title: The Four Men
posts.hook: They met in the back of a restaurant that's still open. You can eat there.
posts.script:
They met in the back of a restaurant on the docks.
A dockmaster who controlled what came off the boats. A woman who ran every bar on the waterfront and never once appears in the official version of this story. A man from the block who owned the only trucks. And one more.
They agreed to stop competing, and inside three years they were richer than the city government.
The restaurant is still there.
You can eat there. The back room's usually booked.
shots: a warm restaurant back room, empty
a checkered tablecloth and four chairs
posts.caption: Four people. One back room. The restaurant's still open.
posts.cta: Would you sit at that table?
posts.shareTrigger: Real-world texture makes fiction feel local.

posts.title: The Woman Nobody Mentions
posts.hook: One of the four founders was a woman and three families have quietly written her out.
posts.script:
One of the four was a woman.
She ran every bar on that waterfront, which meant she knew everything about everyone, which is a more valuable asset than trucks or docks and all four of them knew it.
She's in the photograph. She's on the document.
And she is in almost none of the versions of this story the families tell now.
Work out which crew has been quietly editing her out for fifty years, and you've learnt something real about them.
I'll come back to her.
shots: an archive photo, a woman at a bar, back to camera
a bar mirror, gold light, no faces
posts.caption: One of the four founders was a woman. Three families have edited her out.
posts.cta: Which crew do you think did it?
posts.shareTrigger: Injustice + a puzzle — extremely strong comment driver.

posts.title: Like Brothers
posts.hook: Two men agreed to split it fifty-fifty. Neither of them let go of the handshake.
posts.script:
Two crews at a table. A fifty-fifty split, agreed — and I want to get the wording right here — like brothers.
Neither man let go of the handshake first. It went on long enough that people looked away.
And afterwards the older one leant over to his son and said: Cain and Abel were brothers.
You remember how that ended.
They are going to be in the same building in November.
So are you.
shots: two hands gripped, gold vs pink light
a warehouse half-lit gold, half pink
posts.caption: "Cain and Abel were brothers. You remember how that ended."
posts.shareTrigger: Prediction bait — people commit to an answer publicly.

posts.title: What 1974 Sounded Like
posts.hook: The year all this started, the number one record in this city was about somebody leaving.
posts.script:
The year those four signed that document, the biggest record in this city was a break-up song.
I find that funnier than I should.
When I score the fifty-years-ago material, that's the palette — warm, analogue, a bit of tape hiss, strings that mean it.
And when we come back to now, the room gets its four stations back.
You'll hear the decades move.
That's the actual job on the night: I'm not playing a set, I'm playing a timeline.
shots: a reel-to-reel spinning, warm light
a 1970s radio, glowing dial
posts.caption: I'm not playing a set that night. I'm playing a timeline.
posts.shareTrigger: DJ-craft content — respect from the music audience.

posts.title: Why They Split It
posts.hook: They didn't split the key because they were fair. They split it because they were scared.
posts.script:
People assume the four keys were about fairness. An equal share, one each, very civilised.
It wasn't that.
Each of those four men was certain the other three would take the lot the second his back was turned — and each of them was right.
So they built a door that made betrayal physically impossible. Four turns, one minute, or nothing opens.
That vault isn't a bank.
It's four men holding each other hostage, in steel, for fifty years.
shots: four coloured key-turns, macro
a lock ring, four segments, glowing
posts.caption: It's not a vault. It's four men holding each other hostage in steel.
posts.shareTrigger: Reframe — a sentence people quote back.

posts.title: The Blueprint
posts.hook: The vault's design was never filed with the city. Somebody made sure of it.
posts.script:
A vault that size needs permits. Excavation, structural, electrical — a paper trail six inches thick.
McGraw went looking for it.
There is no record that vault was ever built. No permit, no inspection, no contractor, no invoice. The building above it has full documentation going back to 1969, and underneath it, officially, there is soil.
Somebody didn't just build it quietly.
Somebody went back afterwards and removed it from the city's memory.
shots: a filing drawer, one gap in the folders
architectural plans, a blank section
posts.caption: Officially, there is no vault. Officially, that's soil.
posts.shareTrigger: Conspiracy escalation — feeds the theory crowd.

posts.title: Can I Come Alone
posts.hook: Yes. And you'll leave with a crew, because that's structurally what this night does.
posts.script:
Can you come on your own?
Yes. And I'd say this is one of the few nights where it genuinely doesn't matter.
The second you pick a colour you're on a team with a few hundred strangers who want the same thing you do, and by the third game you'll be shouting at people you've never met.
That's not me being romantic about it. It's structural.
The whole night is built to turn a room of individuals into four crews.
You'll walk in alone. You won't stay that way.
shots: a single figure entering a colour-lit room
strangers reacting together, wide
posts.caption: Come alone if you want. You won't stay alone.
posts.cta: Send this to someone who never goes out.
posts.shareTrigger: Inclusion — reaches the people your ads miss.

posts.title: The Gold Key
posts.hook: The first family took the gold key and immediately did something nobody expected.
posts.script:
The Corvettis took the gold key in 1974 and did something none of the others expected.
Nothing.
No attempt, no approach, no quiet conversation about maybe getting three of the four together. Fifty years of absolute stillness.
The other families read that as weakness for about a decade.
Then they worked out what it actually was.
The Corvettis are the only family that has never once given the other three a reason to move against them.
That's not passivity. That's the longest game anybody in this city has ever played.
shots: a gold key in a drawer, macro
a still gold-lit room, dust in light
posts.caption: Fifty years. They never once tried. That's the strategy.
posts.shareTrigger: Debate prompt with two defensible sides.

posts.title: The Don At Thirty
posts.hook: Before he was the quietest man in the city, he was the loudest man in the room.
posts.script:
There's a version of Salvatore Corvetti most people have never heard about.
At thirty he was loud. Genuinely loud — a shouter, a table-thumper, the kind of man who settled things immediately and badly.
Then in 1981 something happened that he has never discussed, and afterwards he never raised his voice again.
Not once. Not in forty-plus years.
Everybody in this city has a theory about 1981.
Nobody has ever asked him.
shots: an old photo of a young man, gold light
an elderly hand, a pinky ring, still
posts.caption: In 1981 he stopped shouting. Nobody's ever found out why.
posts.shareTrigger: An open loop you can pay off much later.

posts.title: Nothing Written Down
posts.hook: "Nothing written down, nothing said twice." That's not caution. It's a whole worldview.
posts.script:
Overheard in a back room on the docks, from a man explaining to his son how the family works:
Nothing written down. Nothing said twice.
People hear that and think it's about the police.
It isn't. Write it down and it can be taken. Say it twice and you've admitted the first time didn't land.
That family has run on those six words for three generations.
And it's why the only crew in this city with no paper trail is also the only one that's never been raided.
shots: an empty notepad, gold light
a hand, a cigar, a still room
posts.caption: "Nothing written down. Nothing said twice."
posts.cta: Would you survive in that family?
posts.shareTrigger: A quotable rule — screenshot fodder.

posts.title: Doo-Wop And Menace
posts.hook: There's a reason mob films use love songs over violence and it works on you every time.
posts.script:
There's a trick every mob film uses and it works on you every single time.
Put something warm over something terrible. A crooner, strings, three-part harmony — and underneath it, the worst night of somebody's life.
Your ear says safe. Your eye says run.
That gap is where the whole gold station lives, and it's why I play it the way I do on the night.
When you hear something beautiful in that room, check what's happening on the screens.
shots: a warm-lit room, one violent shadow
a record spinning, slow, close
posts.caption: Warm music over a bad room. Works every time.
posts.shareTrigger: Film-nerd bait — pulls a whole adjacent audience.

posts.title: The Respect Economy
posts.hook: One crew in this city measures wealth in favours. It's the hardest currency there is.
posts.script:
The Corvettis don't really deal in money.
They deal in favours — given, owed, remembered — and money is just how they keep score afterwards.
It's the hardest currency in this city because you can't seize it, you can't trace it, and you can't stop owing it by paying.
Half the businesses on those docks think they're independent.
They're not. They just haven't been asked yet.
On the night, gold plays exactly like that. Quiet, patient, and then suddenly you owe them.
shots: a handshake in gold light, no faces
a restaurant, full tables, warm
posts.caption: You can't seize a favour. That's why they still have everything.
posts.shareTrigger: Uncomfortable-question format — high reply rate.

posts.title: The Receipt
posts.hook: McGraw found one receipt in twenty years. It's for flowers.
posts.script:
In twenty years, McGraw has found exactly one piece of paper connecting anybody to the fourth signature.
A receipt. Annual, same date, same florist, going back further than the shop's own records.
White flowers. Delivered to a grave with no name on it, in a plot that was paid for in cash in 1982.
That's it. That's his entire physical evidence.
A man who doesn't exist has been sending flowers to somebody for forty years.
McGraw sits in that cemetery every year on that date.
Nobody's ever come.
shots: white flowers on an unmarked grave
a florist receipt, macro, aged
posts.caption: A man who doesn't exist sends flowers to a grave with no name. Every year.
posts.shareTrigger: Emotional mystery — the strongest myth post in the run.

posts.title: Timings
posts.hook: Doors, story, games, and the part where the whole building loses it. In that order.
posts.script:
The shape of the night.
Doors open, you get your colour, and for the first while it's just a good room and good music while everybody arrives.
Then the story starts, and from there it alternates — music, story, game, music — all night, and the games get bigger.
The last one is the vault, and that's the loudest the building gets all night, by a distance.
Then we come down, we count it, and somebody's crew walks out having won the whole thing.
Come early. The first game matters more than people think.
shots: a clock face, neon reflection
a room filling up, wide, colour-lit
posts.caption: Come early. The first game matters more than people think.
posts.cta: What time are you getting there?
posts.shareTrigger: Practical + urgency; reduces late arrivals.

posts.title: The Pink Key
posts.hook: The second key changed hands in 1987, violently, and the city pretended not to notice.
posts.script:
The pink key didn't pass down. It was taken.
In 1987 the family that held it had a bad year — three funerals in five months, all officially unrelated — and by the spring somebody new was holding it and nobody asked how.
The city's official position was that nothing had happened.
The Halcóns have held it ever since, and they are the only crew whose claim rests on something everybody can remember.
Which is exactly why they're the loudest.
You don't have to shout when nobody doubts you.
shots: a pink-lit marina, 80s haze
a newspaper page, three obituaries
posts.caption: The pink key wasn't inherited. It was taken. In 1987.
posts.shareTrigger: Moral argument — genuinely divides a comment section.

posts.title: Rico's Arrival
posts.hook: He came to this city with nothing and made sure everybody watched him get everything.
posts.script:
Rico Delgado arrived here with nothing and made absolutely certain the whole city watched him acquire everything.
That's not vanity — or it's not only vanity.
If you come up quietly, people can pretend you're not there and take it back. If you come up loudly enough, taking it back means admitting they let it happen.
He made himself impossible to remove without embarrassment.
The white suit, the tiger, the mansion you can see from the bridge — all of it is armour.
Expensive, ridiculous, and it has worked for twenty years.
shots: a white suit under pink neon
a mansion lit up, seen from a bridge
posts.caption: The suit, the tiger, the mansion. It's not vanity. It's armour.
posts.shareTrigger: Reframes a joke into strategy — earns respect.

posts.title: Say Goodnight
posts.hook: Somebody shot at him in his own house. He didn't duck. He complained.
posts.script:
A round went past Rico Delgado's face, close enough to feel, in his own front room.
He didn't duck. He didn't move.
He turned to his tiger and said: you believe this, Sugar? After everything I do for this city?
Then he looked back at the window and said the line he says.
He wasn't frightened. He was offended.
That's the difference between him and everybody else in this story, and it's going to matter in November.
shots: white suit, calm, tracer streaks past
a tiger on a white couch, unbothered
posts.caption: "You believe this, Sugar? After everything I do for this city?"
posts.shareTrigger: Character-defining + a direct question.

posts.title: La Onda
posts.hook: This station is the reason your neighbours know when the party started.
posts.script:
La Onda, 98.6.
Miami synth, gated drums, sax that has no business being that confident, and then it drops into modern Latin and the room doubles.
This is the loudest, sweatiest station on the dial and it is completely unapologetic about it.
Every other crew's sound is trying to tell you something.
This one's just trying to make you move, and it's very rarely wrong.
When the pink station comes up on the night, you'll know without looking.
shots: pink neon, palms, heat haze
a crowd, hands up, sweat, motion blur
posts.caption: The loudest signal on the water. No apologies.
posts.cta: Your one La Onda record — go.
posts.shareTrigger: Request bait; builds your actual crate.

posts.title: Loud Versus Quiet
posts.hook: Two crews have opposite theories about power and by November one of them is wrong.
posts.script:
There are two theories about power in this city.
The Corvettis think it's quiet. Never explain, never repeat, let people work out on their own that they shouldn't.
The Halcóns think it's loud. Be so visible that moving against you is a public act.
Both have worked for decades.
They've never had to be tested against each other on the same night, in the same room, over the same thing.
In November, they will be.
One of those theories is about to be wrong.
shots: gold room and pink room, split frame
two bosses squaring off, colour-split
posts.caption: Quiet power or loud power. One of them is about to be wrong.
posts.shareTrigger: Binary identity — instant, low-effort engagement.

posts.title: The Permit
posts.hook: There is a legal permit in this city for one privately owned tiger. It's real.
posts.script:
Here's something that isn't a rumour.
There's a permit on file for one privately owned big cat. Filed correctly. Renewed annually. Fees paid on time, every time, for nine years.
One crime family in this city has never filed an accurate tax return, has three open investigations, and has been raided twice.
And their tiger paperwork is immaculate.
McGraw has read that permit more times than he'd like to admit, looking for a mistake.
There isn't one. It's the only clean document in this entire case.
shots: an official permit, stamped, macro
a tiger, calm, regal, unbothered
posts.caption: Three open investigations. Immaculate tiger paperwork.
posts.shareTrigger: Absurd detail — the kind people read out loud.

posts.title: Photos
posts.hook: Take photos. There's a booth. Your crew card is the flex.
posts.script:
Take photos. Please.
There's a booth, it's branded, and it will make you look considerably more dangerous than you are.
And you'll have a crew card on your phone all night with your member number on it — which, when you come back, still says how long you've been in.
That's the flex. Not that you went. That you were early.
Post them. Tag them. I look at all of it.
The people in the photos from the first one are going to be insufferable about it for years, and honestly, they'll have earned it.
shots: a branded photo booth, neon
a crew card on a phone screen
posts.caption: The people at the first one are going to be insufferable about it. Rightly.
posts.shareTrigger: FOMO + status; drives first-event urgency.

posts.title: The Cyan Key
posts.hook: The third key was given away, and that's never happened in this city before or since.
posts.script:
The cyan key is the only one that was given.
Not inherited, not taken, not bought. In 1974 the man from the block was handed it by the other three because they needed his trucks and they assumed he'd be the easiest to remove later.
He wasn't.
Three generations on, his family still has it, and they're the only ones who've never had to defend it, because there's never been a version of this city where the block would let them lose it.
They got underestimated on day one.
They've been living off that ever since.
shots: a cyan-lit street corner, night
an old truck, chrome, archive feel
posts.caption: They handed it over because they thought he'd be easy. Fifty years later.
posts.shareTrigger: Underdog vindication — the most satisfying arc there is.

posts.title: Big Deal
posts.hook: He got the name as a joke. Then he made everybody use it seriously.
posts.script:
Marcus Wells got called Big Deal as an insult.
He was nineteen, he'd just refused to do something that everybody expected him to do, and somebody older said it across a room to get a laugh. It got the laugh.
He kept the name.
Used it on everything, said it about himself, never once acknowledged it had been a joke — and inside about four years everybody in this city was saying it with a straight face.
That's the whole man in one story.
He doesn't argue with you. He just outlasts you.
shots: a calm man leaning on a lowrider
a fresh fade, one gold chain, hard light
posts.caption: The name was an insult. He kept it until everybody said it straight.
posts.shareTrigger: Origin story with a real lesson — highly saveable.

posts.title: We Never Had A Lookout
posts.hook: "The lookout's asleep." There was no lookout. He'd eaten the nachos of a man who does not exist.
posts.script:
Four in the morning, an alley, a job about to happen.
One man reports that the lookout is asleep, the light's on a timer, and they're good to move.
Then adds that he also ate the lookout's nachos.
His boss points out, patiently, that they never had a lookout.
Long pause.
"…RIP the nachos, then."
These are the people you're going to be working for in November.
shots: a dim neon alley at 4am
a searchlight sweeping a wall
posts.caption: "We never *had* a lookout, Problem." "…RIP the nachos, then."
posts.shareTrigger: Pure comedy — the highest-velocity post type in the run.

posts.title: Double Nostalgia
posts.hook: Play the original, then the record that sampled it. The room recognises both and feels clever.
posts.script:
Here's a move I'll use all night and I'm telling you now so you can catch it.
Play the original. Let it land. Then drop the record that sampled it thirty years later.
Half the room knows one. Half knows the other. Both halves feel clever, and for about eight bars two generations of people are having the exact same night.
That's the whole cyan station in one trick.
It's also, if I'm honest, the reason I do this job.
shots: two records side by side, one older
a mixed-age crowd, all reacting at once
posts.caption: Play the original. Then play what sampled it. Watch the room split and re-join.
posts.cta: Best sample flip of all time. Go.
posts.shareTrigger: DJ-craft + a music argument that never ends.

posts.title: Joined, Not Recruited
posts.hook: Three crews take people. One crew has people turn up.
posts.script:
Three of the four crews in this story recruit the way you'd expect. Pressure, money, or a debt you didn't know you had.
The Street Kings have a waiting list.
People turn up. From the block, from outside it, from families who'd rather they didn't. Nobody leans on anybody.
The other three find that genuinely confusing, and it's the single biggest advantage anybody in this story has.
On the night, cyan will be the easiest colour to pick and the hardest crew to beat.
Those two facts are the same fact.
shots: a queue outside a cyan-lit door
a crowd, arms round shoulders, laughing
posts.caption: Three crews take people. One has a waiting list.
posts.shareTrigger: Faction recruitment with a genuine argument behind it.

posts.title: Bought, Not Given
posts.hook: The fourth key was sold in 2011, and the paperwork is perfect, which is the suspicious part.
posts.script:
The violet key changed hands in 2011 and — unlike everything else in this story — there's a complete paper trail.
Bill of sale. Transfer of interest. Signed, witnessed, filed, taxed.
That's the part McGraw can't get past.
Every other transaction in fifty years of this has been a handshake, a funeral or a threat.
This one has a receipt.
Either The Firm are the only honest crew in this city.
Or they wanted somebody, someday, to be able to prove it was legally theirs.
shots: a stamped legal document, violet light
a glass tower lobby, empty, cold
posts.caption: Fifty years of handshakes. And one perfect receipt.
posts.shareTrigger: Detective logic — invites the audience to reason.

posts.title: Getting In
posts.hook: Accessible, seated areas, and nothing in the games needs you to move.
posts.script:
A real answer for anybody who's been burned by an interactive night before.
Everything on the night happens on your phone. Every game can be played sitting down, standing still, from a booth, from the back, from wherever you're comfortable.
Nothing requires you to get to a stage, race anybody physically, or be quick on your feet.
There's seating, there's step-free access, and the screens are placed so you can follow the story from anywhere in the room.
If you want to play hard and not move much, this is genuinely the format for it.
shots: a seated group playing on phones
screens visible from the back of a room
posts.caption: Every game can be played sitting down. That's by design.
posts.cta: Send this to whoever needs to know.
posts.shareTrigger: Access post — earns real goodwill and reaches carers.

posts.title: The Buy-In
posts.hook: In 2011 somebody offered a family more money than the family was worth.
posts.script:
In 2011, the family holding the fourth key got an offer.
Not a threat. An offer — more money than the entire family was worth, in cash, immediately, with no conditions except one.
They said yes.
And everybody in this city has spent thirteen years arguing about whether that was cowardice or the single smartest decision anybody in this story has ever made.
They're out. They're rich. Nobody's looking for them.
Meanwhile the other three are about to walk into a building in November and risk everything.
shots: a briefcase of cash, violet light
an empty family home, lights off
posts.caption: They took the money and walked. Cowards or the only smart ones here?
posts.shareTrigger: Moral dilemma — the format that always fills comments.

posts.title: Preston
posts.hook: He's never stolen anything with his hands. He'd like you to know that's the innovation.
posts.script:
Preston Ashford Sterling the Third has never personally taken anything.
He finds that important. He'll tell you it's the innovation — no masks, no guns, no risk, just a proprietary infiltration solution currently in private beta.
What he's actually built is a company that can afford to be patient, and in this city that's genuinely more dangerous than a gun.
He is also, and I cannot stress this enough, extremely annoying.
Both of those things are true and the second one is why people underestimate him.
shots: a black turtleneck, violet server glow
a phone in hand, over-lit face, close
posts.caption: "No masks. No guns. A proprietary infiltration solution."
posts.cta: Every industry has one. Name yours.
posts.shareTrigger: Recognition comedy with a real point underneath.

posts.title: Legacy Infrastructure
posts.hook: Three crime families were described, in a meeting, as legacy infrastructure.
posts.script:
In a meeting, on a slide, a man referred to three multi-generational crime families as legacy infrastructure.
Out loud. To their faces. With a laser pointer.
And the worst part — the genuinely unforgivable part — is that they didn't have a response, because on that particular metric he wasn't wrong.
They've hated him ever since, and none of them can articulate why in a way that doesn't prove his point.
That's The Firm's whole method.
Be insufferable, be correct, survive.
shots: a slide deck in a dark room, violet
three unimpressed silhouettes at a table
posts.caption: He called three crime families "legacy infrastructure". With a laser pointer.
posts.shareTrigger: Contrarian bait — the reply guys arrive immediately.

posts.title: Cold Rooms
posts.hook: Some music is built to make a room feel expensive and slightly unwelcome.
posts.script:
There's a kind of record that makes a room feel expensive and slightly unwelcoming at the same time.
Too clean. Too precise. Nothing in it that sounds like a person.
That's the violet sound and I mix it deliberately cold on the night, because it's the only station on that dial that isn't trying to be your friend.
And here's the uncomfortable bit — it's the one people dance hardest to at four in the morning.
Say what you like about The Firm.
They understand exactly what you want when you stop pretending.
shots: a sterile room, one cold moving light
a late crowd, precise, hypnotic
posts.caption: The only station on the dial not trying to be your friend.
posts.cta: Cold techno at 4am — yes or no?
posts.shareTrigger: Music opinion with a built-in argument.

posts.title: The Keys Are Moving
posts.hook: For the first time in fifty years, all four keys have left the buildings they were kept in.
posts.script:
Something changed this month.
For fifty years those four keys sat in four different places and never moved. Safety deposit, floor safe, wall, whatever each family does.
All four of them have moved.
Not at once. Over about nine days, quietly, and every family thinks their move went unnoticed.
None of them did.
Which means all four crews now believe the same thing at the same time — that this is finally happening — and every one of them thinks they're the only one who knows.
November.
shots: four safes, four hands, four colours
a black car pulling away, wet street
posts.caption: All four keys moved this month. Every crew thinks they were the only one.
posts.shareTrigger: Plot escalation — signals the campaign is going somewhere.

posts.title: The Lead
posts.hook: After twenty years, McGraw got something. He's been sitting on it for a week.
posts.script:
McGraw got something.
I don't know what. I know he's had it for eight days, I know he hasn't filed it, and I know he hasn't told the one person at that precinct he actually trusts.
He's been to that cemetery twice this week. Off-duty. Both times in the rain.
Twenty years of nothing and now he's sitting on something on his own, which tells you it's either the biggest thing he's ever had —
or it's something he doesn't want to be true.
With McGraw it's usually both.
shots: a detective alone in a parked car, rain
an unmarked grave, wet flowers
posts.caption: Twenty years of nothing. Now he's sitting on something and hasn't told anyone.
posts.shareTrigger: Cliffhanger on the audience's favourite character.

posts.title: Tickets
posts.hook: Tickets are up. First one's in November and there is exactly one of it.
posts.script:
Tickets are up.
One night, November, one room, and I'm going to be honest with you about capacity: this format only works at a certain size. Too few and the games don't roar. Too many and nobody can see the screens.
So there's a number, and when it's gone it's gone, and I'd rather tell you that now than do the countdown thing at you later.
If you've been following this since the docks and the four signatures —
you already know more about that room than most people who'll be standing in it.
Come and use it.
shots: a ticket link on a phone, neon
doors closing on a lit room
posts.caption: Tickets up. One night, one room, one number.
posts.shareTrigger: Rewards the long-time follower — converts the serial.

posts.title: The Last Time
posts.hook: All four families were in one room once before. Nine people went in and it ended in under four minutes.
posts.script:
All four families have only been in one room together once since 1974.
Nineteen ninety-eight. A funeral. Neutral ground, everybody armed, everybody behaving.
It lasted under four minutes.
Nobody has ever said what was said. Three of the four people who spoke are dead now, and the fourth doesn't discuss it.
What's on record is that all four families left by different doors and none of them have been in the same building since.
Until November.
When they'll all be in one, on purpose, with you.
shots: an old church, four black cars outside
four doors, four exits, archive feel
posts.caption: Last time all four were in a room it lasted four minutes.
posts.shareTrigger: History + dread — builds real anticipation for the event.

posts.title: Dutch McGraw
posts.hook: Twenty years, no arrests, and he's the only person in this story I actually like.
posts.script:
Detective Dutch McGraw. Twenty years on one case, zero arrests, one trench coat.
He's been passed over four times. He's been told to drop it twice, formally, in writing. His wife left, partly over this. He keeps a toothpick in his mouth because he stopped smoking the week he took the case and never quite stopped needing something.
He is the only genuinely honest person in this entire story.
And it has cost him absolutely everything.
I hope he gets it. I don't think he will.
shots: a rumpled detective, red-blue light
an old case file, dog-eared, thick
posts.caption: Zero arrests in twenty years. The only honest man here.
posts.shareTrigger: Empathy — this is the character people get attached to.

posts.title: Twenty Years
posts.hook: "Twenty years I've been asking the wrong questions to the wrong guys."
posts.script:
Overheard in a lineup room, from a man who has said the same thing to himself every year for two decades:
Twenty years I've been asking the wrong questions to the wrong guys.
And then, quieter — not tonight.
He says it every time. He's said it in front of five suspects, four of whom were in crews and one of whom had wandered in off a dance floor and was holding his booking number upside down.
He pointed at that one.
He always points at the wrong one.
shots: a lineup wall in silhouette
a toothpick jabbed toward the lens
posts.caption: "Twenty years asking the wrong questions." He says it every time.
posts.shareTrigger: Sympathy + prediction; short and quotable.

posts.title: The Scanner
posts.hook: There's a fifth signal on that dial and it isn't music.
posts.script:
There's a fifth signal on the dial and it isn't music.
Scanner chatter, siren stabs, and dispatch static — and on the night I use it as a texture, not a track. When the heat goes up in the story, it bleeds into whatever's playing and the room feels it before anybody's told them anything.
That's the point of scoring a night like this rather than just playing it.
You'll never consciously notice the scanner.
You'll just get tense, and not know why.
shots: a police scanner, red-blue light
blinds, siren light sweeping a wall
posts.caption: There's a fifth signal on that dial. It's not music.
posts.cta: Ever noticed a DJ making you nervous on purpose?
posts.shareTrigger: Craft reveal — makes the audience feel let in.

posts.title: The Gala
posts.hook: The President just announced a gala. Guess which building.
posts.script:
It's official. There's going to be a gala.
A night of unity, he's calling it. A city standing together against crime. Podium, banner, applause, the lot.
And it's in the building.
The same building. The one with the thing underneath it that nobody has permits for.
Every crew in this city got an invitation this week, and every crew knows the other three did too.
So now it's not a question of whether they'll all be in the same room.
It's a question of what they each think they're walking into.
shots: a WAR ON CRIME banner going up
four invitations, four colours, macro
posts.caption: A night of unity. In that building. Sure.
posts.shareTrigger: The plot turn the whole serial has been building to.

posts.title: The Invitation
posts.hook: Four invitations went out. There's a fifth name on the list nobody can account for.
posts.script:
The guest list leaked. Of course it did — it's a political event, they always leak.
Four crews. Four invitations. All accounted for.
And one more name that nobody at that office can explain, that nobody remembers adding, that came through with no contact details and no RSVP required.
One letter.
The organisers assume it's a typo.
McGraw does not assume it's a typo.
shots: a guest list, one line highlighted
an empty chair at a set table
posts.caption: Four crews. Five names on the list.
posts.shareTrigger: The myth confirmed as present — huge escalation.

posts.title: If You're Late
posts.hook: The story runs on a clock. Miss the first twenty minutes and you'll spend the night behind.
posts.script:
If you're late, you'll still have a great night. But I'd rather be straight with you.
The opening sets up who everybody is, and the first game is where your crew starts scoring. Miss it and you'll spend the rest of the night one step behind people who didn't.
There's no penalty. Nobody's going to make you feel bad.
You'll just be the person going "wait, which one's the tiger guy" at eleven o'clock, and your crew will not have patience for you.
Come early. Get your colour. Get the open.
shots: doors opening, a lit foyer
a wristband, a phone, a drink
posts.caption: Miss the open and you'll spend all night going "which one's the tiger guy?"
posts.cta: Who in your group is always late?
posts.shareTrigger: Group-callout — tags happen automatically.

posts.title: The Donor List
posts.hook: The President's biggest donors are four organisations that officially don't exist.
posts.script:
The President's campaign filings are public, which is the funny thing about all of this.
His four largest donors are registered as consultancies. One's registered at a restaurant on the docks. One at a marina office that's been closed since 2019. One at a corner store. And one at a glass tower where the listed director is a man who has never been photographed at work.
None of this is hidden.
It's just filed correctly, and nobody reads filings.
That's the actual lesson of this whole story: the biggest things in this city are hiding in public.
shots: campaign filings, four highlighted lines
a podium, flags, TV lighting
posts.caption: His four biggest donors are registered at a restaurant, a closed office, a corner store and a tower.
posts.shareTrigger: Satire that lands as real — travels beyond the audience.

posts.title: Diamante
posts.hook: He says he knows all the criminals personally. He means it as a qualification.
posts.script:
President Maximillian Diamante will tell you nobody in this country is tougher on crime than he is, because he knows all the criminals personally.
Great people. Total winners.
He says it as a qualification. Like it's a CV line.
And the genuinely upsetting thing is that it works — because it's true, and because saying it out loud is somehow more disarming than hiding it.
He's going to stand at a podium in November under a banner about a war on crime, with every criminal in this city holding a drink behind him.
And he's going to get applause.
shots: a bombastic figure at a podium
four envelopes into a jacket, neck-down
posts.caption: "I know all the criminals personally. Great people. Total winners."
posts.shareTrigger: Political satire — the widest-reaching format here.

posts.title: Fine Patrons
posts.hook: He got to the word 'patrons' and had to pause, because four envelopes went in at once.
posts.script:
At a rehearsal, reading from a script, a man practised the line: I have never, ever taken a dollar from any of these fine—
And then stopped. Because in the actual room, at that exact moment, four envelopes in four different colours were going to be going into his jacket simultaneously.
He asked whether the timing could be adjusted.
He did not ask whether the envelopes could be.
Four more years.
shots: a rehearsal, empty ballroom, one podium
gold, pink, cyan and violet envelopes
posts.caption: He asked if the timing could be adjusted. Not the envelopes.
posts.shareTrigger: Satire with a punchline — the most shareable joke format.

posts.title: State Broadcast
posts.hook: There's a sixth signal and it's brass, flags and absolutely nothing underneath.
posts.script:
The sixth signal on the dial is the State Broadcast, and it is entirely brass.
Campaign-ad fanfare, national anthem energy, applause that isn't there.
I use it for exactly one thing on the night: undercutting. It comes in over the top of something genuinely sinister and it makes the sinister thing funnier and worse at the same time.
That's the trick with satire in a room like that.
Don't tell people it's ridiculous.
Play the fanfare and let them notice.
shots: flags, a podium, TV-broadcast light
a brass section, archive feel
posts.caption: Don't tell people it's ridiculous. Play the fanfare and let them notice.
posts.cta: Best use of pomp in a film — go.
posts.shareTrigger: Craft + film argument; pulls the cinema crowd.

posts.title: All Four Said Yes
posts.hook: Every crew RSVP'd within six hours of each other. None of them are going for the canapés.
posts.script:
All four crews RSVP'd inside six hours of each other.
Think about what that means. Four organisations who have not been in the same building since a funeral in 1998 all decided, on the same afternoon, that they were definitely attending a political fundraiser.
None of them are going for the canapés.
All four know the vault is under that room. All four are bringing a key. And all four have worked out that the other three will be doing exactly the same thing.
They're not sneaking in.
They're walking through the front door in black tie, and so are you.
shots: four RSVPs, four colours, macro
four black cars converging on one building
posts.caption: Four crews. One building. Nobody's sneaking. Black tie.
posts.cta: Which door are you coming through?
posts.shareTrigger: The heist frame lands — this is the ticket-driver.

posts.title: Four Minutes
posts.hook: The vault's window is four minutes long, once a night, and only one person knows why.
posts.script:
Here's what McGraw worked out that nobody else has.
That vault doesn't just need four keys. It needs them inside a window — and the window happens once a night, for about four minutes, when the building's systems cycle over.
Which means it isn't enough for all four crews to be there.
They have to all be there, together, ready, in the same four minutes, having agreed something.
Four organisations who despise each other.
Cooperating precisely, on a clock, once.
That's the actual heist. Not the stealing. The agreeing.
shots: a building's systems cycling, lights dip
a clock face, four minutes marked
posts.caption: The hard part isn't the stealing. It's four crews agreeing for four minutes.
posts.shareTrigger: Reframes the whole story — the smartest post in the run.

posts.title: Bringing People
posts.hook: Bring the friend who says they hate this kind of thing. They're the one who goes hardest.
posts.script:
Bring the sceptic.
Every single time we run something like this, the person who said they weren't going to join in is on their feet by the third game, arguing with strangers about a colour they chose ninety minutes ago.
It's not because the games are irresistible. It's because being on a team is.
The ones who struggle are people who came expecting to sit and watch a show.
The ones who love it are people who came out for a good night and got handed a job.
Bring the second kind. Or bring the first kind and watch it happen.
shots: a group, one arms-folded, then not
a crowd all reacting at once
posts.caption: Bring the friend who says they hate this stuff. They go hardest. Every time.
posts.shareTrigger: Direct tag mechanic with a promise attached.

posts.title: The Weakness
posts.hook: Every vault has a weakness. This one's is that it was designed by people who didn't trust each other.
posts.script:
Every vault has a weakness, and this one's isn't the steel.
It's that four frightened men designed it.
They were so focused on making sure none of them could rob the others that they built something none of them could ever use. Fifty years of eight figures sitting under a building, earning nothing, helping nobody, because the safeguard worked perfectly.
That's the thing about that door.
It has never once failed.
And it has never once let anybody in.
shots: a vault door, seams, one hard light
an empty concrete chamber, distant
posts.caption: It's never failed. It's also never let anybody in. That's the flaw.
posts.cta: Perfect security or a perfect waste?
posts.shareTrigger: Philosophical hook — surprisingly strong on longer platforms.

posts.title: Sugar
posts.hook: She has stolen more from this city's crime families than any human being in this story.
posts.script:
Let's talk about the tiger properly.
Sugar has been present at three of the most consequential meetings in this city in the last decade. She has never been searched, never been questioned, and has never once been considered a participant.
During a fifty-fifty summit between the two most dangerous men in this city, she picked a bag of money off the table and walked out with it.
Neither of them has noticed.
By weight, that tiger has stolen more from this city's crime families than anybody in this story.
And she is the only one who is definitely going to get away with it.
shots: a tiger padding out of frame with a gold bag
an empty spot on a table where a bag was
posts.caption: By weight, the tiger has stolen more than anyone in this story.
posts.cta: Send this to someone who'd get away with it.
posts.shareTrigger: The single highest-velocity post in the campaign.

posts.title: Don't Leave A Dollar
posts.hook: Two bosses said the same four words at the same time and neither enjoyed it.
posts.script:
Two men who cannot stand each other, briefing a job together, arrived at the end of the same sentence at the same moment.
Don't leave a dollar.
They said it in unison. Then they looked at each other with real hatred, because agreeing had felt good and neither of them was ready for that.
That's the thing about November.
They're going to have to cooperate.
And the worst part, for them, is that they might enjoy it.
shots: two bosses, gold and pink light, mid-brief
a smashed neon window, loot falling
posts.caption: They said it in unison. Then hated each other for it.
posts.shareTrigger: Ships the rivalry — audiences adore this dynamic.

posts.title: Blending Turf
